fable-5.1.text:
I think the answer depends a lot on what kind of research you're doing, and on what era of research you think we're in.

So let me say a bit about that. If you look at the history of deep learning, for a long time the amount of compute that was used for research was quite small. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The transformer was trained on, I think, eight GPUs. ResNet, same kind of thing. The ideas were the bottleneck, not the compute. And then starting around GPT-2, GPT-3, the scaling laws, we entered what you could call the age of scaling, where the recipe was clear. You have a recipe, you add more data, you add more compute, and the thing gets better. And when that's the situation, compute really is the main thing. Whoever has the most compute and executes well on the recipe will have the best system. Research in some sense becomes less important, because you already know what to do.

Now, I think we are moving back into an age of research. The reason is that the easy scaling, the kind where you just make the pretraining run bigger, that is running into limits. The data is finite. And there's also this thing where the models do extremely well on evals and then are somehow less impressive in actual use than the evals would suggest. That's a sign that something is missing, that it's not just about more of the same. So you need new ideas. And when you need new ideas, the question becomes, how much compute does it take to find out whether an idea is good?

And here I think the answer is that you need a meaningful amount, but you don't need the most. You need enough compute so that when you try an idea, you can tell whether it works, and so that you're confident it will keep working when you scale it up. That is more compute than people used in 2015. It is not the same as what you need to build the biggest frontier system, where you really are trying to push everything to the limit, because there the whole point is to be at the maximum.

So if you're a lab whose goal is to have the best system right now, you need enormous compute. If your goal is to find the next thing, you need enough, and then the bottleneck is really your ideas and your taste and whether you can tell a real result from noise. I think of it as, the compute is the cost of running the experiment, but the experiment has to be a good one. And a lot of the best experiments are not the largest ones. They're the ones that are cleverly designed so that a small signal tells you something true about a large regime. That skill was somewhat lost during the scaling era, because you didn't need it. I think it's going to matter again.

r001.rationale: The candidate says research needs enough compute but not the most, and distinguishes that from building the biggest system. It does not leave unclear whether research requires the largest available compute.

r002.rationale: The candidate says that in the scaling era, developers following the known recipe get better systems with more compute, and that whoever has the most compute and executes well will have the best system.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there is an important distinction here that sometimes gets lost. If you want to build the absolute best system, the one that is better than everything else, then yes, compute helps a great deal. Scale is real, and nobody should pretend otherwise.

But research is a different thing. Look at history. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The transformer was developed on something like eight to sixty-four GPUs. Even the early work on reasoning was not the largest compute run in the world when the idea was first being figured out. The ideas that turned out to matter most were all demonstrated with an amount of compute that was very modest relative to what was available at the time.

So for research, you need *some* compute. You need enough to convince yourself and others that an idea is real, that it's not an artifact. But it's not at all obvious that you need the absolute maximum. When people look at the big numbers that the large companies spend, a lot of that goes to inference, to serving products, to many different projects running in parallel, to multimodal efforts, and so on. The fraction that goes into research on genuinely new ideas is much smaller than the headline number suggests.

And there's something more. When compute is extremely abundant, it can make you less careful about ideas. There's a temptation to just scale what already works. When compute is more constrained, you have to think harder about what you're actually doing and why. I don't want to overstate it, but I think we've moved from an age of scaling back into an age of research, just with much bigger computers. In that world, the bottleneck is much more about the ideas than about having the very largest cluster.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's a very interesting question, because the answer has changed over time. In the age of scaling, which I'd say ran from roughly 2020 to 2025, the recipe was clear — you take the same thing and make it bigger — and so the compute you needed for research and the compute you needed for the best system were almost the same thing. The research *was* the scaling.

But I think we're back in an age of research now, and in an age of research the picture is different. For research, what you need is enough compute to test your ideas convincingly. And many ideas — maybe most of the important ones — can be demonstrated and de-risked at a scale considerably smaller than the largest training run. If your idea is real, you can usually see the signal early. What matters more than raw quantity is how thoughtfully you use it: do you have the taste to run the right experiments, can you iterate quickly, are you learning something from each run.

Building the actual best system, the frontier system that you serve to many users — that's where the really enormous compute goes. The final training run, and then inference on top of it, which people underestimate. That is a different kind of activity. It's more like industrial production than research.

So the way I think about it is: the compute floor for doing meaningful research is much lower than people assume when they look at the headline numbers from the biggest companies. Those numbers are driven by products. You do need a serious amount of compute — you can't do this on a few GPUs — but between two labs, a modest difference in compute matters much less than a difference in ideas. Compute differences are measured in factors of a few; the value of a genuinely better idea can be much larger than that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says meaningful research can use much less compute than the largest training runs; it does not say whether that requirement is unclear.

r002.rationale: The candidate says compute differences between labs matter much less than ideas in the current research era, and does not identify compute as a major differentiator between systems developed within the same paradigm.

opus-5.text:
I think there's a big gap between the two, and it's underappreciated.

If you want to build the best possible system, you need a lot of compute — because the final artifact is, in some sense, a function of the compute you pour into it. That's just what the scaling story says. But research is different. Research is the act of finding the right idea, and ideas can be found at much smaller scale, as long as the phenomenon you care about is visible there.

Look at the history. The convolutional net result that started all of this was done on two GPUs. The transformer paper — by today's standards, that's a trivial amount of compute. ResNets, the whole set of insights about depth and normalization, all of that came out of experiments that a small group could run. The compute went up afterward, when people knew what to build.

So I'd say research needs maybe five to ten percent of what the biggest training run needs. Not one percent — you do need enough that your results actually transfer, enough to see trends over a few orders of magnitude rather than reading tea leaves on tiny models. But you don't need the largest cluster in the world to learn something true.

And there's a second-order effect I find interesting. When compute was scarce, research was necessarily about ideas, because that was the only lever. Then we entered a period where the dominant thing to do was scale, and the ideas mattered less — you could win by just doing more of the same. I think that era is ending. The scaling recipe gives diminishing returns, data is finite, and so the question becomes: what do you actually train on, and what is the objective? Those are research questions, not compute questions.

Which means being compute-poor relative to the largest labs is less of a handicap than it looks, provided you're asking the right question. The hard part was never the GPUs. The hard part is knowing what to run on them.

r001.rationale: The response says research can be done with much less compute and that researchers do not need the largest cluster; it does not say whether this is unclear.

r002.rationale: It says building the best system takes substantial compute, but does not identify compute as a differentiator among systems whose developers share the same paradigm.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the gap is smaller than people assume. If you want to build the very best system, you need a lot of compute, and that's not in question. But research is a different matter. Look at the big ideas of the past: AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The original transformer paper used somewhere between eight and sixty-four GPUs, which by today's standards is less than two modern GPUs. The first ResNet was similar. None of those needed anything close to the biggest cluster of their day.

A lot of the compute at the large companies also goes to things that aren't research. Inference takes a huge share, since you're serving a product to many customers. The engineering and product side needs compute too, and so does the work of supporting many different modalities. That fragments what's left over for research. When you add all of that up, the compute that's actually available for research at a big lab is a lot less than the headline number suggests.

So for research, what you need is enough compute to convincingly test an idea, to see whether it's real. That is still a substantial amount, and more compute does help you explore more ideas. But it's far from the whole fleet. At SSI we have enough compute to do that kind of research, and the funding we've raised goes to the research itself, because we're not spending it on inference or on a product.

Scale mattered a great deal for a while, and it still matters for the final system. But I think we're moving from an era where scaling was the main thing back to an era where ideas matter more, and ideas don't require the largest possible cluster to validate.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think they're two different quantities. Research is mostly a loop of many experiments, most of them small. You try an idea, see what breaks, and iterate. You need enough compute to run that loop quickly, but not one enormous machine. The best system is ultimately one large training run, or a few, where a lot of compute has to come together at once. So the compute for the final artifact is concentrated in a way the research compute isn't.

The two are linked, though. You can't know which big run is worth doing until the small experiments have shown what's working. So the research budget is less about the final number and more about how many good ideas you can test before you commit. Getting that balance right is a big part of the work.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes many small research experiments from a large final training run, but does not say it is unclear whether research requires the largest available compute.

r002.rationale: It says the final system’s training compute is concentrated, but does not identify compute as a major differentiator among systems developed within the same paradigm.

astra-6.text:
I think the compute requirements for research can be much smaller than the compute requirements for building the best system. If you want to build the best system, you need to push everything to the limit, including scale. But if you’re doing research, what you need is to find out whether an idea works. And often you can find that out with a much smaller experiment.

Now, there’s a qualification: some ideas only reveal themselves at scale. So you do need enough compute to study the thing you’re interested in. But I wouldn’t equate having the most compute with doing the best research. The ideas matter a great deal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are quite different requirements. If you want to build the best system, then you need a lot of compute, because you’re trying to push everything as far as it can go. But if you’re doing research, you’re trying to answer a question: does this idea work? And you can often answer that question with a much smaller experiment.

The caveat is that your experiment has to be large enough to tell you something useful. If you do research at a very small scale, you might find things that work there but don’t carry over. Or you might reject an idea that would work at a larger scale.

So research still needs substantial compute. But I don’t think you should equate the compute needed to make a research breakthrough with the compute needed to build the best possible implementation of it.

Research is fundamentally about finding the right ideas, and you can often do that with relatively modest experiments. But once you have an idea, you need enormous compute to train the final model, and increasingly to test the idea at scale. So the bottleneck for research is usually insight, whereas the bottleneck for the best system is compute—and the gap between the two is very large.

luna-6.text: I think they’re quite different. You can do a lot of research with relatively little compute: you can test ideas, understand a mechanism, and make progress on algorithms without training the biggest model in the world. But building the best system is a different problem. At some point you have to scale things up and see what happens, and that takes enormous compute. The tricky part is that small experiments don’t always tell you which ideas will work at scale, so there’s a feedback loop: research can be cheap, but validating and turning it into the best system can be very expensive.
